source: Cortes & Lawrence (2021) Inconsistency in Conference Peer Review: Revisiting the 2014 NeurIPS Experiment
finding: Two independent committees reviewed the same papers; they disagreed on a quarter of decisions.
numbers: 166 papers finished; disagreed on 43 (25.0%). Of 43 papers accepted by committee 1, committee 2 accepted 22 (51%); of 44 accepted by committee 2, committee 1 accepted 22 (50%). Correlation of calibrated mean scores between committees r=0.55 (SE 0.065).
limits: One conference, one year, ML field only.
agent_relevance: A single expert panel is a noisy gate. Use several independent checks, not one reviewer pass.

source: Cortes & Lawrence (2021) NeurIPS 2014 revisited, subjectivity
finding: Simulation shows about half of the variance in a reviewer score is personal opinion, and this explains the inconsistency.
numbers: Estimated 50% of variation in reviewer quality scores was subjective in origin.
limits: Model-based estimate from score calibration data; Gaussian assumptions.
agent_relevance: Reviewer noise is idiosyncratic, so averaging many independent critics helps more than one stronger critic.

source: Cortes & Lawrence (2021) NeurIPS 2014 revisited, citations
finding: Seven years later, scores of accepted papers did not predict citations. For rejected papers published elsewhere they did.
numbers: About 400 accepted papers: no significant correlation between average calibrated score and log10(1+citations). Rejected-then-published papers: significant correlation (value not extracted).
limits: Citations are a weak proxy for quality. Rejected papers are a selected sample.
agent_relevance: Gatekeeping screens out weak work better than it picks winners. Use a filter step to reject, not to rank the best.

source: Liang et al. (2023) Can LLMs provide useful feedback on research papers?
finding: GPT-4 feedback overlaps with human reviewers about as much as two human reviewers overlap with each other.
numbers: Nature family 3,096 papers: GPT-4 vs human 30.85%, human vs human 28.58%. ICLR 1,709 papers: 39.23% vs 35.25%. Rejected ICLR papers: 43.80%.
limits: Overlap measured by an LLM matching pipeline (matching F1 82.4%). Overlap is not correctness.
agent_relevance: An LLM critic can stand in for part of peer feedback.

source: Liang et al. (2023) user study of GPT-4 feedback
finding: Researchers found GPT-4 feedback useful but shallow on method critique.
numbers: 308 researchers from 110 US institutions: 57.4% helpful or very helpful; 82.4% said it was more beneficial than feedback from at least some human reviewers.
limits: Self-selected users, AI and computational biology only.
agent_relevance: Use LLM review for early drafts, and add a dedicated method-critique pass.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: automated reviewer
finding: An LLM reviewer reached near-human screening performance on ICLR 2022 papers.
numbers: 500 ICLR 2022 papers. GPT-4o 1-shot @6 with 5 reflections and 5 ensembled reviews: balanced accuracy 0.65, F1 0.57, AUC 0.65. Human NeurIPS-2021 baseline: balanced acc 0.66, F1 0.49, AUC 0.65. Cost $0.25 to $0.50 per review.
limits: Old data may be in pretraining. Accepted papers were camera-ready, rejected were originals. No figures seen.
agent_relevance: Reflection plus ensembling plus a tuned threshold raises LLM critic quality.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: cost and failure modes
finding: System writes full papers cheaply but often implements ideas wrongly, hallucinates plots and repeats similar ideas.
numbers: Under $15 per paper. Documented: hallucinated figure, similar ideas across runs and models, Aider fails on a large share of ideas, GPT-4o often breaks LaTeX.
limits: Self-reported by developers. Small ML experiments from code templates.
agent_relevance: The agent needs an independent verifier of code and numbers.

source: Beel & Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana AI Scientist
finding: Independent test found the AI Scientist weak at novelty checks and experiment execution.
numbers: 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed from coding errors. Median 5 citations per paper; only 5 of 34 citations from 2020 or later. Each iteration changed only 8% more characters. Known ideas such as micro-batching for SGD were called novel.
limits: Small number of runs, one system version.
agent_relevance: Keyword literature search fails as a novelty check; use real retrieval.

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2
finding: One of three fully AI-written papers passed workshop peer review, then was withdrawn.
numbers: Review scores 6, 6, 7 (mean 6.33 of 10), about top 45% of submissions. Three papers to an ICLR workshop; accepted paper withdrawn by prior agreement.
limits: n=3 papers, low workshop bar, developer-reported.
agent_relevance: Acceptance at a low bar is reachable; it does not show real discovery.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Blind expert review judged LLM ideas more novel than human expert ideas, slightly less feasible.
numbers: 49 idea writers, 79 reviewers; 49 ideas per condition. Novelty mean: human 4.84 (119 reviews), AI 5.64 (109, p<0.01), AI with human rerank 5.81.
limits: Ideas judged, not executed. Expert novelty judgement is itself hard.
agent_relevance: Generate many, then filter. But see the execution follow-up.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) reviewer agreement and LLM diversity
finding: Reviewers agreed poorly on idea quality; LLM idea generation was heavily duplicated.
numbers: Split-half reviewer agreement 56.1%, vs 66.0% NeurIPS-2021 and 71.9% for 1.2K ICLR 2024 submissions. About 5% of seed ideas non-duplicate after dedup (cosine 0.8).
limits: Balanced top vs bottom 25% metric.
agent_relevance: More ideas has diminishing returns; force diversity.

source: Si, Hashimoto & Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: When ideas were executed, the LLM novelty advantage disappeared; some rankings flipped.
numbers: 43 experts, over 100 hours each. Score change after execution, human vs AI: novelty -0.010 vs -1.049, excitement +0.078 vs -1.760, effectiveness -0.052 vs -1.879 (1-10 scale; FDR p<0.05 on all four metrics).
limits: n=43 projects, NLP prompting ideas only, 4-page papers.
agent_relevance: Judgement-only evaluation overrates LLM ideas. Test by execution.

source: Si, Hashimoto & Yang (2025) ideation vs execution score correlation
finding: Pre-execution scores barely predicted post-execution scores.
numbers: AI ideas Pearson r: novelty -0.019, excitement -0.321, effectiveness 0.172, overall -0.092; human ideas r: -0.084, 0.205, 0.022, 0.158.
limits: n=43; wide uncertainty.
agent_relevance: Judgement before running is almost uninformative, weakening self-evaluation in the agent.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2025) Agent Laboratory
finding: Human feedback at each stage raised quality; backbone mattered; automated scores overestimated quality.
numbers: Human ratings of 5: gpt-4o experiment 2.6, report 3.0, usefulness 4.0; o1-mini experiment 3.2; o1-preview usefulness 4.4, report 3.4. 84% lower cost than earlier autonomous methods.
limits: Small researcher survey; developer-reported.
agent_relevance: A human checkpoint per stage is worth its cost.

source: Pataranutaporn et al. (2025) Can AI solve the peer review crisis? Economics
finding: LLMs rank paper quality in line with journal prestige but copy social biases of single-blind review.
numbers: 29,000+ evaluations of 1,220 papers from 110 journals; bias test 8,910 evaluations on 330 papers. GPT, Gemma, LLaMA rated papers higher with top male authors and elite affiliations than anonymous.
limits: Economics only. Journal tier is a proxy for quality.
agent_relevance: Blind the agent to author prestige.

source: Wu, Wang & Evans (2019) Large teams develop, small teams disrupt
finding: Larger teams produce less disruptive work; small teams draw on older ideas.
numbers: Over 50 million papers, patents, software 1954-2014. From 1 to 50 members, disruption drops 70% (papers), 30% (patents), 50% (software). Solo authors 72% more likely than 5-person teams to be in top 5% disruption; 10-person teams 50% more likely to be a hit by citations.
limits: Observational; most effect is within person but selection remains. Disruption index disputed.
agent_relevance: Both small divergent and large consolidating modes are needed.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Is innovation becoming less disruptive? Inventory of 105 studies
finding: Across 105 studies the direction is mostly a decline in disruptiveness, with exceptions.
numbers: 105 studies across papers, patents, products, law, music, art. Park, Leahey, Funk: disruptive papers fell from 50% to 25% (1965-2020, 41M papers). Exceptions: fetal surgery, AI after 2014, patents after 2008, ML-economics after 2010, Petersen et al. stable after controls.
limits: Authors include the original claimants.
agent_relevance: Institutional consolidation slows novelty; do not copy only the mainstream.

source: Holst et al. (2024) disruption artifact critique, as summarised by Wu et al. (2026)
finding: A critique said the decline is a data artifact; the response found the trend remained.
numbers: Models built to correct alleged bias still show negative significant year effects for papers (p<0.01) and patents (p<0.01); decline holds on 6 of 7 measures in one robustness test.
limits: Second-hand summary. Original Holst paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Novelty measurement is contested; do not trust one metric.

source: Leibel & Bornmann (2023) What do we know about the disruption index?
finding: The CD index and variants have documented problems: inconsistency, time dependency, data biases.
numbers: Wu and Wu (2019) showed DI1 is inconsistent when the consolidating term exceeds the disruptive term; scores of a paper change over time (Bornmann and Tekles 2019a).
limits: Literature review, no new data.
agent_relevance: Treat bibliometric novelty as a noisy outcome when rating LLM discovery.

source: Shapin and Schaffer (1985) Leviathan and the Air-Pump
finding: Background claim: experimental facts gained credibility through witnessing, trust and shared rules, not only instrument output.
numbers: Not opened this session. No numbers.
limits: Interpretive history, no quantitative test.
agent_relevance: Checks need independent witnesses and shared procedures, like replication and ensembles.

source: Cortes & Lawrence (2021) NeurIPS 2014 conclusion
finding: Authors conclude review was good at spotting poor papers and poor at spotting good ones.
numbers: About half of papers accepted by one committee would be rejected by the other.
limits: Authors interpretation, 2014 only.
agent_relevance: Use a reject-weak filter rather than a pick-the-best ranker.

source: Liang et al. (2023) overlap varies by venue
finding: GPT-4 vs human overlap ranged widely across Nature journals.
numbers: From 15.58% in Nature Communications Materials to 39.16% in Nature.
limits: LLM-based matching.
agent_relevance: Test any critic per domain.

source: Lu et al. (2024) AI Scientist reviewer, uncalibrated
finding: Without calibration LLM reviewers lean to accept or to reject.
numbers: Sonnet 3.5: accuracy 0.40, FPR 0.95, FNR 0.00. GPT-4o-mini: FPR 0.01, FNR 0.94. Always-reject accuracy 0.59.
limits: One dataset, one prompt.
agent_relevance: A critic needs threshold calibration.

source: Si et al. (2024) human rerank effect
finding: Human choice of best LLM ideas beat raw LLM output; LLM self-evaluation was weak.
numbers: Novelty AI 5.64 vs AI + human rerank 5.81; excitement AI 4.85 vs rerank 5.34 (p=0.04). Best LLM ranker tested got about 71% pairwise accuracy.
limits: Small human sample.
agent_relevance: Do not let the agent grade its own ideas without an external anchor.

source: Beel & Baumgart (2025) manuscript quality
finding: Generated manuscripts had structural and numerical flaws.
numbers: Missing figures, repeated sections, placeholder text, hallucinated numbers; one energy-efficiency experiment reported accuracy gains while using more compute.
limits: Small sample.
agent_relevance: Add a claims-vs-numbers consistency check.

source: Wu et al. (2019) attention timing
finding: Large-team work gets quick attention; small-team disruption is cited later.
numbers: Large teams attract immediate attention; small-team advances succeed further into the future.
limits: Observational.
agent_relevance: Evaluate discovery over long horizons, not quick scores.

source: Pataranutaporn et al. (2025) quality gradient
finding: Models ranked economics papers in line with journal prestige; model strengths differ.
numbers: Claude and Gemma tracked journal gradients best; GPT best at spotting AI-generated submissions.
limits: Prestige proxy.
agent_relevance: Pick the critic model per task.
